articles.title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
articles.summary: Witnesses say a missile hit a building containing the surgical wards and intensive care units at Nasser hospital, the largest in southern Gaza.
articles.body:
At least six people have been killed and about 20 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital, the biggest in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.

Eyewitnesses told the BBC that a single missile fired by a warplane hit a building containing the surgical wards and intensive care units overnight.

The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizk Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".

The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.

Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".

Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.

Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.

Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.

In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said the missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.

A spokesman for the Civil Defence, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, initially said that five people had been killed and 20 others injured.

Videos shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by the blast.

Local activists have also circulated claims that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.

Speaking to reporters in the aftermath of the strike, the director of Nasser hospital said the building had been hit in a vertical strike, causing extensive damage.

Nasser hospital was hit by a double Israeli strike in August 2025, which killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers.

Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite a ceasefire agreement in October last year.

More than 1,620 people have been killed since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.

The humanitarian crisis in Gaza has recently worsened as a result of heavy rains that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Famed ship heads for afterlife as artificial reef in deliberate sinking off Florida
articles.summary: Nov 11 (Reuters) - Famed ocean liner SS United States, the largest passenger ship ever built in America and the world's fastest, headed for the sea floor nea...
articles.body:
Nov 11 (Reuters) - Famed ocean liner SS United States, the largest passenger ship ever built in America and the world's fastest, headed for the sea floor near Florida on Wednesday in a deliberate sinking designed to transform the vessel into the world's biggest artificial reef.

The finale to a ‌yearlong process preparing the ship to meet its destiny, 75 years after it was first launched at sea, was presented in a livestream with aerial views of ‌the once-grand vessel's rusted hulk, stripped of its two smokestacks, quietly, slowly settling into calm waters of the Gulf of Mexico before succumbing to the deep.

The ship, measuring nearly 1,000 feet (300 m) from stem to stern, was ​surrounded by onlookers and safety crews aboard dozens of tugboats and recreational vessels that accompanied the ocean liner as it was towed out to sea for its final voyage.

By then, work crews had spent months removing all environmentally unsafe materials from the ship, including residual fuel, wiring, glass, ductwork and other non-metal items, as well as any objects that could pose entanglement hazards for scuba divers.

The crews then cut holes strategically throughout the ship's hull and its decks to ensure that it would sink in a gradual, level and uniform manner, according to a fact sheet ‌posted online by project organizers. No explosives were used.

Passageways were ⁠also cut through the 12 decks of the interior to allow for marine life to thrive in and around the ship on the sea floor.

If all goes as planned, the aging 20th-century vessel will come to rest upright on the gulf floor at a depth of 180 ⁠feet off the coast of Destin, Florida, a resort town and recreational fishing haven known for its white sand beaches and emerald green waters. The upper deck is expected to end up about 50 feet beneath the surface, organizers said.

The sinking process began at about 1 p.m. CST but was so imperceptibly slow that the majority of the ocean liner's hull remained well above the surface ​as ​the sun set on the idle ship, surrounded by blinking lights of nearby vessels.

After hours, during which ​the waterline was seen creeping up the ship's hull inches at a ‌time, the sinking accelerated as the sea poured through the holes cut into the lower decks and flooded the interior. In the final moments, livestream footage showed the ship abruptly listing to its port side before gently rolling into the sea and disappearing.

Warren Jones, a spokesperson for organizers, who watched the sinking from an observation boat, said the SS United States would probably take 30 to 60 minutes to reach the seabed once the interior compartments were all completely filled with water.

The SS United States, a wonder of post-World War Two oceanic luxury and engineering that carried the rich and famous across the Atlantic at speeds still unmatched, was retired from service in 1969 amid the rising popularity of commercial air travel.

The ‌vessel sat moored for nearly 30 years in Philadelphia, seemingly destined to be sold for scrap, before ​authorities in Okaloosa County, in Florida's panhandle, stepped in to purchase the ship as part of a $13 million ​project.

"We worked year after year to keep that ship from going to the ​scrap yard," said Jones, a boyhood passenger of the ship and representative of the SS United States Conservancy, a group that sold the ship ‌to Okaloosa County.

After obtaining permission from the US Coast Guard and other ​agencies, the county had the vessel towed to ​a shipyard in Mobile, Alabama, where it was prepared for disposal at sea.

The SS United States will be in good company, joining a collection of more than 500 smaller underwater sites created from the remains of various sunken ships and concrete structures to create a divers' haven known as the Destin-Fort Walton Beach Artificial Reefs.

Speaking ​with Reuters by phone on Wednesday night, Jones said some wreck ‌divers were already gearing up to explore the sunken remnants of the ocean liner as early as Thursday morning.

Jones, recounting vivid memories of riding the ship ​as an 8-year-old passenger with his family in 1961, said he was "comforted seeing it settle on the floor of the gulf and being embraced by ​the sea."

(Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Editing by Stephen Coates and Tom Hogue)

articles.title: Canadian homebuyer loses her entire $70,000 deposit after backing out of a $1.388 million Vaughan property deal over mortgage trouble; court also orders her to pay sellers $35,000
articles.summary: A Canadian court has ordered a homebuyer to forfeit her $70,000 deposit after she failed to complete a $1.388 million property purchase in Vaughan,
articles.body: A Canadian court has ordered a homebuyer to forfeit her $70,000 deposit after she failed to complete a $1.388 million property purchase in Vaughan, Ontario. Reesa Garber had agreed to buy the property from Sharon and Alexander Laraia, with the transaction scheduled to close on July 16, 2024. However, after waiving the financing condition, she later told the sellers that she could not secure the mortgage needed to complete the purchase.She also asked them to terminate the agreement and relist the property to limit potential losses. According to the Canadian Legal Information Institute (CanLII), the Ontario Superior Court of Justice found that her emails amounted to an anticipatory breach of contract and ruled that the sellers were entitled to keep the deposit.Why a $1.38 million home purchase in Vaughan turned into a buyer-seller disputeThe property at 81 Littleriver Court in Vaughan was marketed for sale by Catherine Artenosi, a realtor with Coldwell Banker The Real Estate Centre. Garber, who was a registered real estate agent in Ontario, submitted an offer on April 28, 2024, to buy the property for $1,388,000. The sellers accepted the offer. The agreement required a $70,000 deposit upon acceptance and set July 16, 2024, as the completion date.The purchase was initially conditional on financing until May 3, 2024. On that date, Garber fulfilled the financing condition and removed the financial terms, making the agreement firm. She paid the deposit, which remained in the brokerage’s trust account.On June 13, 2024, Garber contacted the sellers’ listing agent and said she was having difficulty selling her own property and could not secure mortgage financing. She explained that she needed to sell her property to fund the purchase. The agreement did not make the purchase conditional on the sale of her property. The sellers said they would hold her to the contract.The following day, Garber contacted the office of the real estate lawyer, Giancarlo Soppelsa, and repeated that she could not obtain financing and would be unable to complete the transaction on the agreed date.She asked either to terminate the agreement or extend the completion date. The sellers refused both requests and said they expected the purchase to proceed as agreed.Buyer formally backed out of the $1.38 million deal before closingGarber repeated on June 21 that she could not complete the purchase because she had been unable to sell her property and obtain sufficient financing. On June 24, she sent a signed mutual release seeking to end the agreement. In the same communication, she demanded that the sellers immediately re-list the property to mitigate potential damages.She followed up through counsel and, on June 26, again said she would not complete the transaction. The sellers’ lawyer wrote to her counsel on June 27 that her conduct amounted to an anticipatory breach, accepted the breach and reserved the sellers’ right to seek damages and forfeiture of the deposit. Justice André found the messages clear and unequivocal.Court dismissed buyer's claims and ordered release of $70,000 depositThe court rejected Garber’s argument that her attempts to obtain financing and arrange an appraisal revived the agreement. Justice André said the sellers had no contractual obligation to provide access to the property for financing purposes after the agreement had ended.The sellers had offered to revive the transaction on July 3, 2024, on new terms, including an additional $20,000 deposit and a direction releasing the deposit if the purchase failed to close again.Garber did not accept the offer. The judge found that the unsuccessful attempt to revive the agreement did not change the consequences of her earlier breach. The court ordered the release of her $70,000 deposit to the sellers and directed her to pay them $35,000 in costs within 90 days.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available court records published by the Canadian Legal Information Institute (CanLII). articles.title: Concern over Abbey House Museum Victorian street revamp plan
articles.summary: Abbey House Museum in Leeds has released proposals for changes to the recreated Victorian street.
articles.body:
Campaigners have said they are "appalled" by proposals to modernise a Victorian street at a popular museum in Leeds.

The plans, announced last week , showed concept art designed to make the Abbey House Museum in Kirkstall more hands-on and immersive.

Angela Bamfort, who has been visiting the museum since she was a child, said the images - which appear to show an atrium, fairy lights and backless sofas - were more like something she would expect to see in a shopping mall.

Leeds City Council, which runs the attraction, said that the artist's impressions "do not represent finished proposals" and are "a starting point for conversations" about the museum's future.

The museum was initially put forward for closure during the city council's budget proposals in 2024 - but was saved after a "passionate" response to a public consultation.

One of those who fought to save it was Dianne Riding, who died in 2025.

Her daughter Laura Winterlich said: "When my mum died, she was secure in the knowledge that she knew the museum had been saved."

When she saw the plans to modernise the museum, she said her "heart sank".

Riding had worked in education in Leeds for more than 40 years, and taken pupils on trips to the museum.

In particular, Winterlich said she liked showing pupils the representation of the Victorian street.

"A lot of the street scene is very representative of the working-class population of Leeds, which is often very under-represented.

"You have places like Harewood House and Temple Newsam, they are about a select few throughout history.

"But the pub, the school, the small alleyway houses, all of those things are reflective of the average person that most of us would have been."

She is supportive of the museum being modernised, but said that there are other parts of the building that could be improved instead.

"The children's gallery is somewhere that could be extremely engaging and hands-on," she said.

"That's an area that's very neglected by the museum and does need development.

"But it's the street that is the heart of that museum."

Jill Clark has a special connection to the Victorian street, as it was her father and uncle who originally built the set in the 1950s.

"He loved working there, he and my uncle," she said.

"They were very proud of what they accomplished."

After her father passed away, Clark said that she enjoyed visiting the museum and remembering the stories he had told her about building the street.

"It's just lovely to stand there and think, my dad built this."

She first saw the proposals to change the museum on a Facebook post.

"I couldn't believe they would contemplate doing that."

Apart from her own family connection, Clark is also a member of the Friends of Leeds Museums, and attended a consultation last year on the future of Abbey House.

"There were lots and lots of ideas about what could be done with the museum," she explained.

"Not once did anybody mention changing the streets."

Angela Bamfort, 62, is particularly fond of the Victorian areas.

"It's like stepping into another world," she said.

"Especially when you go downstairs into the streets with the little shops and the cobbled road.

"The proposal looks like something that should be next door to the Trinity Centre.

"I think it's absolutely appalling, it just shouldn't be done.

"How on earth do you modernise it and keep it a Victorian museum?

"I don't think we'll be visiting if these plans go ahead."

A spokesperson for Leeds City Council said that a public event was held last weekend where representatives from the museum and the council discussed the future vision for the site with those in attendance.

"Further consultation and engagement" will take place before any formal proposals and funding bids are submitted, they added.

The council acknowledged that the Victorian street in particular is a popular part of the museum, and said they want to "strike the right balance between enhancing the visitor experience while preserving what we know our visitors love".

"We hope that by working together we can enhance and improve the museum so it can continue to welcome visitors for many years to come."

articles.title: Winchester event set to introduce boys to choral singing
articles.summary: Choristers or Quiristers are young singers who typically sing in church choirs or cathedrals.
articles.body:
Choral singing has been a part of tradition in Winchester for centuries - and with their red coats and high notes, the Pilgrims' School's Choristers and Quiristers are keeping it alive.

The search for the next generation of boys to have a "life-changing singing opportunity" is underway.

Winchester College, Winchester Cathedral and The Pilgrims' School are joining forces to launch their Be a Chorister Day.

The event on Saturday is designed to give boys ages six to 10 a chance to experience the chorister lifestyle for an afternoon, to potentially join other children on choral scholarships.

Choristers and Quiristers are young singers who typically sing in church choirs or cathedrals.

Alongside regular services, choristers all over the country take part in events including carol concerts at Christmas and Easter, concert tours to other countries, and recording for radio and television broadcasts.

The choristers of Winchester have sang on actor Sir Anthony Hopkins' album, which reached the top of the classical album chart, and have recorded music for a Nintendo soundtrack, featuring in the Star Fox 2026 score.

Emma Short, registrar at the Pilgrims' School, said about the event: "Boys will have the chance to dress up in cassocks, sing alongside current Choristers and Quiristers, and ask plenty of questions".

Organisers said boys do not need any formal music experience to come along and don't need to be able to read sheet music or playing instruments.

Headmaster Tim Butcher said: "The benefits that come from being a C or a Q, as we call them, can be truly life-changing."

He cites the advantages of taking up singing as being gaining skills in performance, presentation and teamwork. He also said it can grant children a sense of confidence and purpose.

"I hugely encourage parents and boys to come and learn more about whether this could be the right route for their son.

Be a Chorister takes place on Saturday 14 November. The day starts at Winchester College, with a stop at Pilgrims' School and ending with a finale Evensong in Winchester Cathedral.

articles.title: Bracknell artists concerned as AI use leads to fewer commissions
articles.summary: Artists Luke Crump and Emi Giovanini from Bracknell say more companies are using AI for flyers and posters.
articles.body:
Independent artists have said that finding work in the era of AI "is a struggle".

Artificial Intelligence has rippled through the creative industries, so Berkshire-based Luke Crump and Emi Giovanini have opened a month-long exhibition for people to enjoy their art free of charge.

Giovanini said that before AI she would get a lot of commissions for logos and flyers but that "since AI came all the people, especially with low budgets, try [using AI]" instead, taking work away from local creatives.

She has had to find different ways to earn an income, but said: "AI will never take away things from us 100% because we are still people.

"We're still humans, and it's art made by humans.

"AI can't replicate someone creating a mirror, for example, which is something that we do a lot."

While showcasing their art in the community is important, it includes hidden costs such as the rent for the venue or the commission charged by venues.

Crump said that when he and Giovanini were looking for a venue for the Monsters and Mischief exhibition "you start to look behind the nice facade".

"The white walls and things like that, you quickly realise that they can take a lot, and sometimes up to 50%, which is a lot for a small independent artist," he added.

The Bracknell couple found Other Space Arts, a non-profit community interest company venue that hosts independent artists and musicians.

Based in Windsor, it was opened by Matt Flemming and his wife in 2025 for small artists to use their space.

Flemming said: "For the exhibitions, we always give the artists completely free hire of the space. We just ask for a small 10% commission back on any work sold."

He said AI can be "a wonderful tool in certain aspects".

But added that with it becoming more of a concern to the creative industry, spaces like Other Space Arts become "more important" because "what AI can't do is create connections amongst humans".

Dominic Lees, associate professor at the University of Reading and specialist adviser to the Digital Culture Media and Sport (DCMS) Committee at a House of Commons inquiry into British film and high-end television, said: "The AI industry has got this original sin.

"They've already stolen from the creative industry."

He said that when companies were training their AI models "they were sending bots out onto the internet to scrape anything they wanted, including copyrighted material, made by creative artists and using that to train their models".

Lees said that it has led to artists "competing against their own AI-generated images".

He added that the UK has a good copyright regime but "with AI, there's no enforcement of that.

"Even when AI companies are breaching copyright, there's no mechanism to force them to give compensation or to force them to retract," he said.

A DCSM spokesperson said the government has engaged "extensively" with creatives and AI firms to ensure that they take the "right approach to this issue".

They added: "Copyright laws must protect the UK's position as a creative powerhouse while unlocking the extraordinary potential of AI-driven innovation to grow the economy and improve lives."

articles.title: In 1984, Paul Newman gave his Rolex to his daughter’s boyfriend, saying it “tells pretty good time”; 33 years later, it sold for $17.75 million
articles.summary: Discover how a gifted Rolex from Paul Newman became one of the most expensive wristwatches ever sold, fetching $17.75 million at auction 33 years after it was given away.
articles.body: A casual question about the time on a Connecticut riverbank led to one of the best-known watch sales in history. In the summer of 1984, Paul Newman asked his daughter Nell’s boyfriend, James Cox, what time it was. Cox said he did not own a watch, so Newman handed him the Rolex on his own wrist. Cox kept the watch for roughly 33 years. In October 2017, he and Nell Newman consigned it to Phillips in New York, where it set a world record for a wristwatch at auction. Newman had died in 2008 and never saw the resale.Joanne Woodward gave the Daytona to Newman in 1968The watch was a gift from his wife. UPI reported that Joanne Woodward gave him the Cosmosgraph Daytona in 1968. The case back was engraved “Drive Carefully, Me”, a nod to Newman’s racing. Newman put it to work. He timed races with it and bet friends that it ran more accurately than theirs, a habit Phillips has described in its sale notes. He would call the speaking clock, a phone line that gave the exact time, to get his money. Phillips also indicated that he wore this watch daily from 1969 to 1984.Cox met Nell Newman in the fall of 1983 at College of the AtlanticThe two started dating while they were both still fellow students. She went by the name Nell Potts in school, but hid her association with her family. According to Phillips, the girl only came clean about her surname after listening to a particular story. In the summer of 1984, the two were staying at their family estate in Westport, Connecticut. In her letter to Cox that accompanied the watch, Nell stated that her father went to the riverbank to see how James was doing. One day he asked Cox what the time was and Cox told him he did not know and had no watch. Newman gifted him the Rolex and explained that all he needed to do was to wind it daily and then “it tells pretty good time”.In some versions of the story, the quote has changed to “keeps good time”, which is the version published in City AM. UPI also mentioned that Cox had responded to the question “a hair past a freckle,” his way of saying he had no watch.The watch seemed to vanish after 1984Collectors were completely oblivious about the whereabouts of the watch. According to Autoblog, it appears to have been lost in 1984 when Newman got a new Daytona watch from his wife. NBC Los Angeles also says that the watch went off the radar and was assumed missing, following the death of Paul Newman in 2008. All along, Cox owned it. It is said by Phillips to be one of the greatest mysteries in horology that was only solved when Cox came forward.The Daytona sold for $17,752,500 on October 26, 2017The watch was auctioned by Phillips in New York on October 26, 2017. According to Phillips, the 1968 Cosmograph Daytona Reference 6239 reached a hammer price of $15.5 million. Phillips claimed that their final price was $17,752,500, including the buyer’s premium and thus they achieved a world record for an auctioned wristwatch. As stated by Hodinkee, the former recorded for the most expensive wristwatch, which sold for approximately $11.1 million in 2016, was held by the steel Patek Philippe Reference 1518. That made the Newman Daytona about 60 percent more expensive.A portion of the proceeds went to Nell Newman’s foundation and Newman’s Own Foundation The watch was listed for sale by both Cox and Nell together and according to UPI, Cox is the treasurer of the Newman Foundation. According to the report by KOMO News, Cox was going to donate a major part of the money he earns to the Newman Foundation. The Newman Daytona held the record for just over two years, from Phillips’ sale on October 26, 2017 to the Christie’s Geneva auction on November 9, 2019. Christie's reported that on November 9, 2019, the steel Patek Philippe Grandmaster Chime Reference 6300A-010 sold for 31 million Swiss francs, about $31.3 million, at the Only Watch charity auction at Christie’s Geneva. The same report also notes that the price topped the Newman Rolex’s $17.8 million. The Newman Daytona still ranks as the most expensive Rolex sold at auction.You use AI every day. articles.title: It is time for a change of leadership in the Democratic Party in the US
articles.summary: The Democrats need to deliver on an ambitious agenda, and they need new energy and new voices to do so.
articles.body:
American voters sent a clear message in the midterm elections: They want things to change. They want to pay their bills without worrying every month. They want affordable housing, groceries and healthcare. And they do not want the United States pulled into another war.

That message was aimed at the Republicans, who are in power. But Democrats need to hear it too. If we think winning the midterms means we can go back to business as usual, we may be in for a rude awakening in 2028.

People want results. They want leaders who understand what it means to choose between paying rent and filling a prescription. And if we are serious about changing our policies, we have to be willing to change our leadership.

That is why I believe Senator Chuck Schumer should step aside as the Senate Democratic leader. It is time for veteran Democrats to make space for younger, more energetic members who managed to galvanise the electorate with a message focused on ordinary people and change.

Schumer has spent nearly 50 years in elected office. I respect that service. He knows Washington, and experience matters. But experience cannot be the only qualification. If we keep telling younger Democrats to wait their turn, when exactly does their turn come?

This is not just about age. It is about whether the people who built the party’s old playbook can recognise when that playbook no longer works.

Too often, Democrats have been more comfortable talking about what is possible in Washington than what is necessary in people’s lives. Longstanding ties to major donors and corporate interests can make that problem worse. The influence of groups such as the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, has also become a point of disagreement within the party, particularly over US policy towards Israel and the wider Middle East. Younger Democrats are asking whose voices get heard when the party sets its priorities.

That does not mean every longtime Democrat is controlled by donors or every young Democrat is a socialist. But the party’s growing progressive and democratic socialist movements are pushing questions that cannot be brushed aside: Why are homes so expensive? Why does healthcare still put families into debt? Why do powerful interests seem to get a hearing before ordinary workers?

The party also needs to be honest about the 2024 elections. Democrats did not lose simply because of one leader or one issue. They failed to connect strongly enough with voters’ everyday concerns. Donald Trump promised relief from high prices and an end to costly foreign entanglements. Many voters were willing to give him another chance. That should have been a warning to the party about how much affordability and peace matter.

But saying, “Make life affordable,” is not enough. In the next Congress, Democrats should put real bills on the table: measures to lower prescription drug costs, strengthen access to healthcare, expand affordable housing, support first-time homebuyers and tackle price gouging when the evidence warrants it. We should be prepared to explain what each proposal would cost, how it would work and how families would benefit.

That means making choices. It may mean challenging donors and interest groups that prefer the status quo. It also means working with Republicans when a deal genuinely helps people, without allowing compromise to become an excuse for abandoning the promises that brought Democrats to power.

I have been involved in politics long enough to know that changing leaders will not magically lower grocery bills. But leadership sets the agenda. It decides which bills get a vote, whose ideas get a hearing and which fights are worth having.

Independent voters are watching. Some supported President Trump in 2024. Some supported the Democrats in last week’s midterms. That does not mean the same people all switched sides. It does mean neither party owns their loyalty. Delivering on promises gives Democrats a chance to earn their trust; failing to deliver gives them every reason to look elsewhere in 2028.

Schumer deserves credit for his years of service and for the party’s recent Senate gains. But I believe the party needs a new voice at the top of the Senate and new energy that can steer the party towards delivering on an ambitious agenda of making life affordable again.

If we want voters with us in 2028, we have to give them a reason to stay. Not another slogan. Not another promise to wait. Real changes in people’s lives, and leaders willing to make them happen.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina must return to Bangladesh to face her sentence
articles.summary: Delhi should ensure that its territory is not used to incite violence in Bangladesh or threaten its people.
articles.body:
For families who lost relatives in Bangladesh’s July-August 2024 uprising, Sheikh Hasina’s presence in India is far more than just a question of political refuge. Some are caring for injured relatives, while others have been left devastated by their losses. Parents have rooms that are now empty. When the ousted prime minister speaks to Bangladeshis from India, the question arises: Why should those who paid the price for democracy have to watch the very person they hold responsible for their suffering continue to intervene in Bangladesh’s politics from abroad?

In February 2025, the UN Human Rights Office estimated that as many as 1,400 people may have been killed during the 2024 uprising, with thousands more injured. It identified systematic repression by the former government, the security forces and violent elements of the Awami League, and concluded that there was an official policy of violent suppression that warranted further investigation into potential crimes against humanity. These were international findings of fact, not a criminal verdict.

Subsequent domestic proceedings dealt with individual responsibility. In November 2025, Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity, including instigating and abetting the atrocities and ordering lethal force against protesters. It also held her responsible under the doctrine of superior command responsibility and sentenced her to death in absentia. She has called the trial politically motivated. Her denial in no way diminishes the victims’ right to justice. Bangladesh has requested her extradition from India, but she remains there.

Under Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, the government is attempting to repair a damaged economy and to re-establish a political culture that has been badly scarred by years of autocratic rule. Yet Hasina’s supporters abroad continue to promote the prospect of her political comeback on social media. Such messages fuel uncertainty about the future of Bangladesh’s democratic transition, particularly for families still waiting for justice.

The elected government and all political organisations committed to that transition have a responsibility to defend it. They should respond to any attempts to destabilise it with factual information and legal action, keeping victims at the heart of their policies. But Bangladesh cannot address these concerns alone while Hasina remains in India.

In an interview with Prothom Alo, C Christine Fair, a political scientist at Georgetown University, said that Hasina had been useful to India and that New Delhi would not hand her over. But India’s decision to shelter Hasina is one issue; allowing her to continue intervening in Bangladesh’s politics from Indian territory is another.

In January 2026, Bangladesh’s Foreign Ministry accused Hasina of inciting violence to disrupt the forthcoming elections after she addressed a public event in New Delhi. Fair questioned why New Delhi appeared unwilling to restrain Hasina when it had previously persuaded foreign political figures, including the Dalai Lama and Aung San Suu Kyi, to exercise restraint. She suggested that India’s domestic politics explained the difference. From Bangladesh’s perspective, this raises questions about how much weight New Delhi gives to its neighbour’s concerns when they conflict with its own political calculations.

Whatever political considerations shape New Delhi’s position, Bangladesh’s extradition request must be assessed on its legal merits. A person’s political status does not automatically prevent extradition. Article 6 of the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty specifically excludes murder, incitement to murder and a number of related offences from the political offence exception. Other grounds and safeguards for refusal remain applicable.

Through sustained diplomatic engagement, the government of Bangladesh should make clear that Dhaka wants constructive relations with India on the basis of sovereign equality and expects a serious response to its extradition request. It should also ask New Delhi to ensure that its territory is not used to incite violence in Bangladesh or threaten its people. Specific incidents should be documented, and peaceful political expression should be clearly distinguished from calls for violence.

If India is serious about resetting its relationship with Bangladesh, it has to respect the democratic mandate of that country and acknowledge the suffering of its people. Protecting a former dictator from accountability will only serve to increase mistrust. Sheikh Hasina must return to Bangladesh to answer in person for the killings and abuses committed under her government and to face any further lawful proceedings. Her return must deliver justice to the victims and help restore the rule of law that Bangladesh is so keen to re-establish.

articles.title: Indonesia vice president resigns amid dispute over eligibility
articles.summary: Gibran Rakabuming Raka, son of former President Joko Widodo, resigns as court questions his overseas education.
articles.body:
Indonesia’s vice president has resigned in the midst of a scandal over his high school diploma, adding pressure on a government facing widespread dissatisfaction over the economy, corruption and wildfires.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka submitted his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto and parliament on Thursday, the speaker of the People’s Consultative Assembly told reporters.

Speaking hours later at ⁠a press ⁠conference ⁠alongside Gibran at the Presidential ‌Palace, Prabowo ⁠said he had accepted ‌the resignation with ⁠a “heavy heart”.

Gibran is the eldest son of former President Joko Widodo, Prabowo’s immediate predecessor.

“There will always be political dynamics in public office, that’s normal,” Widodo told reporters from his hometown in Solo after the resignation, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.

“We will continue to support President Prabowo’s government, especially programmes that serve the interests of the broader public,” the former leader said.

Gibran, 39, leaves office after serving two years of his five-year term as questions grew over his eligibility after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.

Under Indonesia’s Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy does not trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People’s Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.

Gibran had offered to resign on Tuesday during a meeting with the president, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy.

But a cabinet minister said Prabowo urged Gibran at the time to defend himself, and it wasn’t clear whether he had accepted the resignation offer.

Indonesia’s vice president does not have many constitutionally defined powers apart from acting as the president’s representative at official events and taking over if his boss is incapacitated.

The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents Gibran submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements. His critics have accused him of never receiving a high school diploma.

A subsequent petition submitted on Wednesday to the leaders of the House of Representatives by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties began a parliamentary process that could lead to Gibran’s impeachment.

Under Indonesian law, House leaders must establish a special committee to examine whether Gibran has violated the constitution by serving as vice president despite allegedly failing to meet election requirements.

If lawmakers determine there is sufficient basis for the accusation, the House must ask the Constitutional Court to rule on whether a constitutional violation has occurred.

Gibran’s downfall comes as thousands of protesters have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest economic hardship, corruption, perceived authoritarianism and the government’s handling of months of devastating wildfires emitting a toxic haze that has made thousands of people ill.

It also comes amid investigations into allegations that top police officials were involved in wiretapping targeting the president. The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to the wiretapping scandal.

articles.title: Israel strikes another hospital in Gaza; 6 killed, over a dozen injured
articles.summary: An Israeli airstrike targeting Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a doctor, and wounded at least a dozen others, according to
articles.body: An Israeli airstrike targeting Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a doctor, and wounded at least a dozen others, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. The strike hit the hospital's surgery department early Thursday, damaging parts of the building and raising fresh concerns over the safety of medical facilities in the war-torn Palestinian territory.The Israeli military confirmed carrying out the strike, saying it had targeted "a senior Hamas terrorist" and other militants allegedly operating inside the hospital complex. However, it did not provide evidence to support the claim.An Associated Press journalist at the scene reported that parts of the hospital's second floor had been destroyed in the attack. The Gaza Health Ministry said the strike hit the surgery department, with a doctor among those killed.Nasser Hospital, located in Khan Younis, is one of the few medical facilities still functioning in Gaza, where years of conflict have severely damaged the healthcare infrastructure and left hospitals struggling to cope with casualties and shortages.Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups of using hospitals and civilian infrastructure as cover for military operations. The Israeli military has also targeted the Nasser Hospital complex in previous attacks.In 2025, an Israeli strike on the hospital killed five journalists, including Associated Press contributor Mariam Dagga, after hitting a gathering point used by local reporters at the complex.The latest attack comes amid continued Israeli military operations in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement reached between Israel and Hamas in October 2025. articles.title: Netanyahu’s legacy: Personality politics reshapes Israeli democracy
articles.summary: Netanyahu’s fight for political survival turns the parliament’s opening into a scene of insults and acrimony.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for a national unity government – at least among Jewish Israelis – during the swearing-in of Israel’s new parliament, or Knesset, on Tuesday, hoping to cling to power. The opposition to him, which now has a majority of seats but has yet to form a government, reacted with heckles, catcalls, and walkouts.

Citing supposed internal and external threats, Netanyahu called for unity with the opposition bloc that has been tasked with forming a government to replace him. Netanyahu pointed to the threat posed by Iran and the increased number of democratically elected lawmakers who are Palestinian citizens of Israel, whom he accused, without evidence, of seeking Israel’s destruction.

“We must do one thing – set aside every other consideration and form a national unity government. Only such a government will be able to meet challenges of this magnitude. It is impossible to handle them with a narrow government,” he said of the potential for a minority government that many analysts consider likely after coalition negotiations are complete.

“I say this because here in this parliament they are seriously talking about forming a narrow government like this, a government that includes within it terror supporters, haters of Israel, or that would be dependent on them,” he said, referring to the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Even by the standards of Israeli politics, where analysts say personality has long overshadowed party and policy, Tuesday’s session was unusually contentious.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett heckled Netanyahu while trading barbs with the latter’s wife, Sara, and his hard-right ally Itamar Ben-Gvir, while many of the Palestinian lawmakers attacked by the prime minister during his speech walked out in protest.

Gadi Eisenkot, who has been given the first chance to form a new government , subsequently cancelled previously scheduled coalition talks with Netanyahu and declared him “unfit for office”.

Netanyahu has long played an outsized role in Israeli politics, helping transform the political system into one that is highly based on personalities, with voters typically identifying a leader they like first, and then focusing on policy discussions. Nevertheless, despite having contributed more to that change than any other politician, Netanyahu now finds himself fighting for his political life.

If Eisenkot is able to form a viable new government – which still hangs in the balance – Netanyahu faces being frozen out of power, and a future in which his corruption trial continues without the protection of the prime minister’s office. There will also likely be an inquiry into his and his government’s failings in the run-up to the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023.

His potential downfall, however, does not mean an end to personality politics in Israel. Instead, it may be one of the most lasting parts of his legacy, said Roi Zur, an Israeli specialist in voting behaviour and election strategies at the University of Essex.

“Netanyahu Americanised the party system in Israel and made Likud a populist party,” he said of the influences the country’s longest-serving prime minister has had on Israel and his own party.

“It is a clear case in Israel that the person at the head of the list or the head of the party is very important, and politics evolve around the head of the party,” Zur said. “We see it in how people think about political parties or voting in general in Israel. When you ask people, ‘Who are you voting for?’, they say, ‘I vote for Netanyahu, I vote for Bennett, I vote for Eisenkot,’ whilst in the past it was ‘I vote for Likud, I vote for Labor,’ and so on.”

Dahlia Schneidlin, an American-Israeli pollster, noted that Israeli political campaigns had become more personalised in the past few decades even though elections in the country are almost all based on voting for a party slate, and not individuals.

That had led to many cases where voters focus on the personality rather than the party, and vote accordingly.

However, the Israeli electoral system almost always leads to coalition governments. And bringing other parties into a coalition often needs leaders to demonstrate “political neogitiating and bargaining skills”, Schneidlin said, as they try to encourage others to join them.

Eisenkot, Schneidlin said, will have to demonstrate those skills if he is to form a government, rather than simply being focused on his own personality.

But the emphasis on differences in political personality over policy positions has fuelled a culture where personal differences, such as those between Netanyahu and opposition stalwart Avigdor Lieberman – whose shared animosity is well known but whose right-wing political positions are in some ways very close – contribute to a populist politics easily understood by a public eager to see itself as politically engaged.

“The stress on the personal makes everything so much worse,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, said. “With party structures so centralised, leaders can become almost dictatorial and get to act without constraint. This is how it becomes possible for a prime minister to accuse 19 elected members of the Knesset of being terrorist sympathisers and nobody thinks it’s extraordinary. It’s become toxic,” he said.

articles.title: A Colorado delivery driver who cares for her 82-year-old mother apologised at a door for a mixed-up pizza order, the family came out and prayed with her, and strangers have since donated over $76,000 to help her
articles.summary: More than $76,000 has been raised for a Colorado woman who works as a pizza delivery driver while looking after her 82-year-old mother.
articles.body: More than $76,000 has been raised for a Colorado woman who works as a pizza delivery driver while looking after her 82-year-old mother. The fundraising campaign began after a family she delivered an order to learnt about her responsibilities and decided to help her.Suzanna Metcalf's situation came to public attention after a brief interaction at the home of Pastor Neal Seiwert in Castle Rock, Colorado, Good News Network reported. She had arrived with an incorrect pizza order and apologised to the family. She told them she would have to return with the correct order and blamed the mistake on getting old.The family chose not to focus on the delivery mix-up. Seiwert, his wife Hailee and their three young daughters stepped outside to pray with Metcalf. They placed their hands on her shoulders during the prayer. The interaction was recorded by a doorbell camera.The video was later shared online by Seiwert and reached millions of viewers. Its popularity brought attention to Metcalf's circumstances, particularly the responsibilities she manages outside her delivery job.She works delivery shifts while serving as the full-time caregiver for her 82-year-old mother. Her responsibilities include managing her mother's daily care and medical needs, as well as household expenses. The Seiwert family decided to extend their support beyond the prayer after learning more about her situation.Family starts fundraiser with Metcalf's permissionAfter the video attracted widespread attention, the Seiwerts managed to locate Metcalf. They then approached her about starting a fundraising campaign and received her permission to do so.The GoFundMe page described Metcalf as a woman who had spent years putting others first. The family set an initial target of $10,000, hoping to provide some financial assistance as she continued looking after her mother.However, contributions continued to arrive well beyond that target. More than 2,600 donors have contributed to the campaign over the past year. The total has now crossed $76,000.The money is intended to give Metcalf some financial breathing room while she manages her caregiving duties and delivery work. The campaign's response followed the widespread circulation of the doorbell camera footage.Pastor speaks about the response to the videoSeiwert later discussed the incident with the New York Post. He said his family wanted Metcalf to know that they were there to support her and that other people valued her efforts too.He also spoke about the emotional response from people who watched the recording. “So many people are commenting on how it brought them to tears. articles.title: Pope Leo welcomed by millions in his second ‘homeland’ of Peru
articles.summary: On his Latin America tour, the pontiff is expected to spend 3 days in Chiclayo, where he was bishop from 2015-2023.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has been welcomed by a few million people upon his arrival in Peru, his adopted homeland, for the final leg of a three-nation Latin American tour, just weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

People waving flags and wearing pope-themed shirts filled the main plaza in Lima and erupted into loud cheers as a big screen showed the plane touching down on Wednesday local time. Some held signs that read, “Welcome home”.

A Vatican statement said three million people greeted the pontiff in Lima, setting another record for the biggest crowd of his papacy after an estimated 2.5 million people attended an outdoor Mass in Buenos Aires earlier this week.

The 71-year-old travelled to Uruguay and Argentina before heading to Peru.

The pope was born in Chicago, the United States, but served in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop for two decades and obtained citizenship there, before being tapped to lead the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics.

The pontiff said his return to Peru held “a very special meaning”.

“Today, I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” he said at Lima’s Gran Teatro Nacional. “I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am returning to my homeland.”

Peru prepared for the homecoming by erecting a 14-metre (46ft) statue of Pope Leo with outstretched arms, towering over a seaside park in Callao. Merchants in Lima were selling pope-themed shirts and souvenirs.

The pontiff is scheduled to spend three days in the northern city of Chiclayo, where he was bishop from 2015 to 2023.

In a closely watched speech to President Keiko Fujimori, whose father Alberto Fujimori led Peru through the turbulent 1990s and a brutal war against Maoist Shining Path rebels, Pope Leo urged the president to build confidence among her people after her narrow election victory earlier this year.

He invited Fujimori to confront the wounds of the country’s turbulent past, alluding to her father’s contested legacy. “Past events deserve to be treated with justice and sensitivity, leaving room for harmony to grow ‌and for differences ⁠to be addressed with respect,” he said.

The pontiff also called on Peruvians to cultivate “honesty, integrity, and a willingness to engage with others”, saying those qualities were essential to sustaining trust and democratic institutions.

In welcoming the pope, Fujimori said his visit was an invitation for Peru to pursue its “unfinished task” of national reconciliation.

When Alberto Fujimori was pardoned in 2017, Leo – then Bishop Robert Prevost – criticised the move, saying the former president should personally seek forgiveness from victims if Peru were to achieve genuine reconciliation.

Pope Leo began the trip less than a month after lung cancer surgery and has appeared in good form, making long speeches in a firm, clear voice.

articles.title: Kampala school deaths: Probe as four Ugandan pupils die in suspected poisoning
articles.summary: The head teacher of the school has been arrested to assist police investigations.
articles.body:
Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.

The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died on Tuesday. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital.

The head teacher at the school, Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre, has been arrested to assist with investigations.

According to the school, eight pupils had eaten oranges shared by a fellow pupil.

Five pupils, including the four who later died, started vomiting. The fifth is still in hospital.

Post-mortem examinations are being carried out to determine the exact cause of death.

A police spokesperson was quoted by local media as saying that detectives would visit the village where the oranges the pupils ate came from.

The centre has been cordoned off as a crime scene.

Ugandan media shared videos of grieving parents describing their children's final moments, with some accusing the school of failing to provide clear and timely information.

The police have offered condolences to the bereaved families and affected community and say more information will be provided in due course.

The tragedy comes at a time when concerns are mounting over health and safety conditions in schools across Uganda.

Previous cases involving suspected contaminated food and exposure to harmful substances have left pupils hospitalised with symptoms including stomach pain, vomiting and breathing difficulties.

The incidents have intensified calls for authorities to strengthen monitoring of school feeding schemes, improve hygiene standards and ensure safer learning environments for children.

articles.body: US vice-president JD Vance is reportedly considering face-to-face talks with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei as he takes a leading role in efforts to negotiate an end to the war.According to The Wall Street Journal, which cited US and Middle Eastern officials and people familiar with the discussions, Vance wrote to Rezaei in October requesting a meeting. However, no date has been fixed, and the two sides continue to communicate through mediators and regional allies.President Donald Trump has told senior aides and counterparts in recent days that he is open to Vance resuming negotiations with Iran, and has authorised him to pursue talks, officials told the newspaper. However, discussions about a possible meeting between Vance and Iranian officials are still at a preliminary stage.US officials said the vice-president has lately been more active in Iran diplomacy than special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who are also involved in negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war.The WSJ reported that Qatar has emerged as a possible venue for the next round of talks. Vance met the Qatari prime minister on Monday, after which the two held discussions with Trump and other White House officials.Efforts to restart negotiations, however, face considerable obstacles. People familiar with Tehran’s position said Iranian officials want Washington to lift its naval blockade, release frozen assets and ease oil sanctions before talks resume. US secretary of state Marco Rubio dismissed these demands as unrealistic, but said Washington would be ready for diplomacy if Iran altered its stance.Mediators have proposed confidence-building measures, including the US moving its aircraft carriers farther away and easing restrictions on Iranian ports. In return, Iran would allow 25 oil tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, Middle Eastern officials told the newspaper.Doubts persist over whether a deal can be struck. articles.title: From fastest passenger ship to world's largest artificial reef: Historic US ocean liner sinks off Florida
articles.summary: A historic US ocean liner, once the fastest passenger ship in the world, was deliberately sunk in the Gulf of Mexico on Wednesday to create what is
articles.body: A historic US ocean liner, once the fastest passenger ship in the world, was deliberately sunk in the Gulf of Mexico on Wednesday to create what is expected to become the world's largest artificial reef.The 990-foot SS United States, which is 108 feet longer than the Titanic, was taken underwater in a controlled operation off the coast of Florida. The $13.5 million project is aimed at turning the former luxury liner into a major destination for divers and fishing enthusiasts, while creating a marine habitat for species such as tuna, marlin and swordfish.The sinking took longer than expected, with much of the ship still visible above the water hours after the operation began. The vessel finally leaned to one side and submerged at around 9 pm local time.“She is an amazing lady who will not lay down without a fight,” Coleen O’Malley, president of Coleen Marine, the company overseeing the sinking, said before the ship disappeared beneath the surface, as quoted by Associated Press. “Much like the amazing nation she was named after.”Officials said the process took longer partly because crews had to fill 128 fuel and lubricant tanks with water to ensure the ship would settle evenly on the ocean floor. “She’s a big ship,” said Nick Tomecek, a spokesperson for Okaloosa County, which helped organise the project.How was the ship sunk?The sinking was carried out without explosives, which officials said could not be used because of federal environmental and explosives regulations. Instead, crews opened the ship's seawater intake system to allow water to flood its hull.Workers had also cut 10-foot-by-10-foot openings in the decks and removed more than 400 portholes in preparation for the operation. The ship is expected to rest in around 180 feet of water, with its top deck approximately 60 feet below the surface, making it accessible to divers.The site is around 25 miles southwest of Destin, Florida, in an area that already has more than 500 artificial reefs.The previous largest artificial reef in the region was the USS Oriskany, a 911-foot aircraft carrier deliberately sunk off Pensacola in 2006. Officials said experienced divers could potentially visit both wrecks in a single day.“We're trying to be the best diving destination in the world,” Tomecek said.Why was the SS United States famous?The ship was a technological marvel when it made its maiden voyage in 1952. Built by more than 3,000 workers in Virginia, it carried around 1,700 passengers on its first Atlantic crossing, including Margaret Truman, daughter of then US President Harry Truman.During that voyage, it averaged nearly 41 mph (66 kph), breaking the speed record held by Britain's RMS Queen Mary since 1938. The record was set despite the ship encountering a gale with winds reaching 69 mph.At 990 feet, the liner was longer than the Titanic, which sank after hitting an iceberg during its maiden voyage in 1912. Over its career, the SS United States crossed the Atlantic more than 800 times and carried prominent passengers, including Hollywood stars Grace Kelly and Elizabeth Taylor, and presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John F. Kennedy. A young Bill Clinton also travelled aboard the ship in 1968 on his way to Oxford University.Passengers were once served elaborate meals, including caviar, roast duckling and smoked ox tongue.“She really embodies and expresses this country’s best,” said Susan Gibbs, the granddaughter of the ship's designer. “She represents pride and resilience and strength and beauty.”The SS United States was decommissioned in 1969. Later efforts to convert it into a hotel or put it to other commercial uses failed, and it remained docked in Philadelphia from 1996 until recently.The reef project was intended to preserve the vessel rather than see it dismantled for scrap. As part of the preparations, its two 65-foot smokestacks were removed and are expected to become the centrepiece of a museum dedicated to the ship.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Ten police officers, 18 fighters killed in northwest Pakistan attack
articles.summary: Officers were returning from a mine in Kohat district when fighters opened fire on them, authorities say.
articles.body:
Gunmen have attacked police officers conducting an operation against illegal gold mining in northwestern Pakistan, with 10 officers and 18 fighters killed in the ensuing violence.

A statement by provincial police in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa said officers were returning from a mine in the Gumbat area of Kohat district on Wednesday when armed men opened fire on them.

In addition to the dozens killed, 12 police personnel were wounded, the statement said.

Hours later, the Pakistani Taliban issued a statement claiming the attack.

Earlier, a senior administrative official in Kohat told the AFP news agency that fighters had set two police vehicles on fire during the assault, while two other police vehicles and one private vehicle were missing.

Another senior administrative official in the Orakzai area of Kohat said that 10 fighters belonging to the Pakistan Taliban were killed during a separate operation in the district.

A large quantity of weapons was also recovered from the fighters, the official said.

A spokesman for a local emergency service said earlier on Wednesday that there had been a “firing incident involving police personnel” in Kohat district, adding that rescue workers were treating a dozen wounded officers.

Security forces are battling intensifying violence in the border province that they say emanates from Afghanistan, an accusation the Taliban government in Kabul rejects.

The Pakistan Taliban, formerly known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, have stepped up attacks on security forces in the region in recent months.

Pakistan has seen a surge in violence in recent years, much of it blamed on the TTP.

The group is separate from but closely allied with the Afghan Taliban, who returned to power in neighbouring Afghanistan in 2021.

Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been fraught since the Afghan Taliban retook power, and worsened after deadly border clashes in October last year that led to near-total closure of the border.

Pakistan frequently accuses Afghanistan’s Taliban government of sheltering TTP fighters, an allegation Kabul denies.

Hundreds of civilians have been killed in fighting between the two countries in the last year, according to figures from the United Nations mission in Afghanistan.

articles.title: Britain's aircraft carrier drone experiment could hold the key to India's next naval leap
articles.summary: The Royal Navy wants to see a collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) fly from one of its aircraft carriers next year, and the experiment could be useful well
articles.body: The Royal Navy wants to see a collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) fly from one of its aircraft carriers next year, and the experiment could be useful well beyond Britain. First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins announced aboard HMS Prince of Wales, at the international sea power conference held in Oslo, that Northrop Grumman's Talon Blue, designated YFQ-48A by the US military, is being prepared for a carrier launch. The jet drone flew for the first time only last month.For India, the interest is obvious, HMS Queen Elizabeth and INS Vikrant share a basic design feature as neither of the two ships has catapults to launch fighters. Both launch fixed-wing fighters from a bow ski-jump ramp, set at roughly 14° on the Vikrant and 13° on the British carrier. The catapult helps launch aircraft from the deck of these massive ships. While on ships such as the INS Vikrant and HMS Queen Elizabeth, aircraft take off under their own power. The ramp helps jets leave the deck with heavier fuel and weapon loads than a flat deck would allow. Both ships also carry an air wing of roughly 30 to 40 aircraft, and both depend on forward speed into the wind to help launches.That is why the British trial matters. If a CCA can be launched from a ski-jump deck and handled alongside crewed jets, it will show New Delhi that the concept works on carriers like its own.India's own effortThe Indian Navy is developing its Naval Collaborative Combat Air Vehicle (N-CCAV), centred on the Abhimanyu platform by Bengaluru-based NewSpace Research & Technologies. The company was selected under the Ministry of Defence's iDEX (innovations for defence excellence) initiative through Innovations for Defence Excellence (ADITI) 2.0, signed a design-and-development contract in April 2025 and displayed a half-scale model at Aero India in February 2025. A proof-of-concept aircraft was targeted for 2026, and these remain targets, not an induction.The unmanned aircraft is meant to fly with the MiG-29K and the Rafale-M, not replace them. The CCAs are expected to take on roles such as surveillance, electronic warfare, decoy and strike-support missions. It could fly ahead of manned fighters, gather information, jam radars or draw fire from air defences. It is expected to work semi-autonomously, with pilots giving high-level commands.Where the comparison stopsThe proof of concept is partial, but the Vikrant uses arrested recovery, this method uses a tailhook to catch one of four wires to safely stop an aircraft as it lands on the deck, while the British carriers are designed for short take-off and vertical landing aircraft. The US Navy though demonstrated the landing of a large unmanned system on an aircraft carrier back in 2013 when the X47-B landed on the USS George HW Bush (CVN 77). The US Navy is also planning to regularly operate the MQ-25A Stingray from its flat tops from 2029 onwards.A successful launch off a ski-jump would help India, but recovery may need its own demonstration. Shipboard storage, handling, maintenance and launch and recovery arrangements for India's CCA will also have to be tested on Indian decks.

articles.title: Was Delhi pollution data during Diwali misleading?
articles.summary: BBC Verify analysis indicates missing data led official Diwali pollution figures to be lower than they should be.
articles.body:
BBC Verify has found significant discrepancies between two Indian government datasets showing Delhi's air pollution during Diwali, indicating official figures may not have captured the full extent of the problem.

As fireworks lit up Delhi's skies on 8 November to mark one of India's biggest festivals, some monitoring stations recorded very high levels of PM2.5, a fine particulate matter which can damage people's lungs and cause other serious health problems.

But every hourly PM2.5 reading above 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre was missing from the widely cited air quality index (AQI) published by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), when compared to data from the Delhi Pollution Control Commission (DPCC).

Delhi is one of the most polluted cities in the world and often has dangerously poor air quality , so it is vital people living in India's capital can trust the official data. Firecrackers are not the only cause of pollution, which is also attributed to a mix of reasons including vehicle emissions, construction dust, farm fires and atmospheric factors. But they can worsen air quality, especially in winter.

The CPCB, whose figures are generally cited by Indian media, has issued a statement which said readings above 1,000 micrograms are treated as "outside" the range for detection its equipment has been calibrated for and are excluded from calculations.

"During extreme episodes which are occasional like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of relevant pollutant for concerned station," the statement added.

Dr Manoj Kumar, a researcher at Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), told BBC Verify that excluding high readings risks misrepresenting actual pollution levels and could cause people to lose trust in official figures.

Our analysis found that, across the same 30 stations over 24 hours covering Diwali night, available CPCB readings averaged 240 micrograms per cubic metre - less than half the average of 551 in DPCC's data.

On the night of Diwali from Sunday into Monday, Delhi's already high pollution levels rose sharply as the celebrations peaked.

Three different pollution monitoring stations recorded PM2.5 hourly concentrations above 3,000 micrograms, DPCC data examined by BBC Verify shows.

Dr Kumar said that even a short-term exposure to extreme levels of particulate matter can have adverse health impacts.

The World Health Organization's air quality guidelines state that annual average concentrations should not exceed five micrograms per cubic metre.

Between 21:00 local time (15:30 GMT) on 8 November and 07:00 on 9 November, during the peak of Diwali celebrations, 217 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 16 stations reported complete data during this period, while 43 had at least one missing observation.

None of the 116 readings above 1,000 micrograms from the 30 DPCC-managed stations appeared in the CPCB's published records they feed data into.

This matters because stations need at least 16 hours of valid PM2.5 measurements to calculate a daily average, according to CPCB's methodology. So a station with too many missing or invalid readings will not contribute to official pollution calculations.

One example of a station with several hours of missing data was at RK Puram in south Delhi, where pollution peaked at nearly 2,500 micrograms.

Using hourly PM2.5 readings from this station, BBC Verify calculated an average concentration of about 945 micrograms over the 24-hour period after 17:00 on 8 November.

But similar averages of CPCB's published data for 14 of those 24 hours produced a much lower figure of 299 micrograms. The missing 10 hours also meant this data was not included in daily average calculations.

The missing data across the city means that, despite a sharp overnight rise in pollution at some monitoring stations, CPCB reported Delhi's AQI at 344 at 16:00 on 9 November, down from 376 at the same time the day before.

Dr Sierra Clark, an environmental epidemiologist from City St George's, University in London, warned classifying high pollution readings as missing could leave out days which "contribute the most to short-term health events, such as asthma attacks and heart attacks".

She told BBC Verify "for transparency", Delhi's pollution reporting could show two scenarios including and excluding extreme pollution episodes.

"The latter would give a sense of typical pollution levels that are more representative of people's day-to-day experience. But it is also important to show the impact of those few days and what they contribute," Dr Clark added.

Pollution in Delhi is not limited to PM2.5 and satellite imagery shows a thick haze over the city on 8 and 9 November.

Satellite measurements of other pollutants like nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO) and fire activity in the atmosphere, rather than at ground level, showed increases on 8 November.

But their overall average for Diwali week was not very high compared with 2024 and 2025.

articles.title: Jamie Dimon warns, as AI companies ‘boast’ their Agents can do a lot including making payments for customers; says: Don’t allow that as they will …
articles.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) developers boast that autonomous agents can manage personal errands, book travel, and even execute purchases, JPMorgan
articles.body: As artificial intelligence (AI) developers boast that autonomous agents can manage personal errands, book travel, and even execute purchases, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon is urging consumers and financial institutions not to allow AI agents to handle direct banking payments. Speaking at The Economic Club of Chicago this week, Dimon cautioned that authorising a software agent to execute payments requires handing over sensitive banking codes and if done, it is effectively inviting unvetted algorithms deep inside personal accounts with no promise that it will protect your best interests.“That means they are in your bank and you’re assuming they’re going to act properly on your behalf and they may not,” Dimon said, warning that autonomous agents could carry out actions that prove “treacherous” for financial institutions.Jamie Dimon highlights dangers of rogue consumer AI agentsDimon’s comments arrive amid rapid commercial adoption of consumer-facing AI agents that are capable of managing personal calendars, drafting emails and coordinating travel bookings. The JPMorgan chief previously sounded alarms during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call, warning that the financial system could soon contend with thousands of rogue agents. Dimon noted that autonomous tools may execute round-the-clock cyber intrusions or trigger vulnerabilities if granted access to consumer accounts.Despite the warnings, JPMorgan is advancing its own controlled implementations. Company CFO Jeremy Barnum confirmed that the lender’s proprietary Smart Cash tool, which has been built to help clients oversee and balance liquidity across multiple accounts, is currently undergoing an early-stage pilot. JPMorgan has used AI internally since 2012 across functions including risk assessment, fraud prevention, marketing, credit underwriting, and customer support.AI is moving ‘more like a Tsunami’Drawing historical parallels, Dimon compared the rapid rise of AI to the Industrial Revolution, but noted that modern computing shifts are occurring at high speeds. Calling the rapid spread of the technology “more like a tsunami” that cannot be stopped, Dimon argued that public institutions and corporate leaders must move quickly to contain digital fallout: “You can’t stop it. You just have to, like, manage the hell out of it.”With open-source releases and systems originating worldwide, Dimon emphasised that global governments cannot simply halt model proliferation. The technology’s acceleration is backed by massive capital flows, with tech giants Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta planning more than $700 billion in capital expenditures this year, primarily dedicated to AI infrastructure.Recently, JP Morgan Chase, Citi Bank and Bank of America ‘banned’ AI agents from logging into customer accounts and moving money. They fear that the software could initiate uncontrolled cash movements and erode vital deposit bases.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Sam Pitroda praises PM Modi, receives Diwali wishes; X user's cheeky request gets a reply
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday extended Diwali and Gujarati New Year greetings to Indian Overseas Congress chief Sam Pitroda,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday extended Diwali and Gujarati New Year greetings to Indian Overseas Congress chief Sam Pitroda, responding to a video in which the Congress leader spoke warmly about his personal equation with the Prime Minister."Happy Diwali and Nutan Varsh Abhinandan to you Sam Bhai and to Anjana Ben. Praying for a joyful and healthy year ahead. Jai Jagannath!" PM Modi wrote on X.The Prime Minister shared a post featuring Pitroda's remarks about their personal relationship, in which the Congress leader described PM Modi as a "Gujarati friend"."He is a Gujarati friend. I respect him as a person. My wife and I have met him. He has been very warm, kind, loving and caring at a personal level. Of course, he is a good orator and hard-working, and we get along well. We have no personal issues," Pitroda said."I have nothing against Mr Modi as a Gujarati leader, friend or well-wisher. He has been very warm towards me, and I appreciate that. Similarly, I have been to his house in Gujarat several times," he added.PM Modi's wishes to Pitroda also prompted a light-hearted exchange on social media. Reacting to the Prime Minister's post, an X user, Mihir Jha, wrote in Hindi, "If you can wish Sam Pitroda a Happy Diwali, wish us one too, Modi Ji."The Prime Minister responded with festive greetings of his own. "Aapko bhi Happy Diwali Mihir Bhai. Have a great festive season and year ahead," Modi wrote, adding a smiling emoji.The warm exchange was a departure from the past, when PM Modi had sharply criticised Pitroda, particularly during the 2024 Lok Sabha election campaign.In May 2024, PM Modi had hit out at Pitroda over his remarks comparing the physical appearances of Indians from different regions to those of Africans, Chinese, Arabs and Europeans.Addressing an election rally in Telangana's Warangal, PM Modi referred to Pitroda as Rahul Gandhi's uncle in America and said he would not tolerate insults directed at Indians on the basis of their skin colour.Pitroda subsequently stepped down as Indian Overseas Congress chairman before being reinstated weeks later.His remarks on inheritance tax in the US had also triggered a row during the election campaign, with PM Modi using them to attack the Congress over its alleged wealth redistribution plans.During the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, too, PM Modi had launched a sharp attack on Pitroda over his "hua toh hua" remark on the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, saying the three words reflected the arrogance of the Congress leadership. Pitroda later apologised.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
