articles.title: US closes a 4-kilometre road twice a year as thousands of snakes, including venomous rattlesnakes and cottonmouths, migrate between a swamp and limestone cliffs with changing temperatures
articles.summary: A road in southern Illinois, United States, has an unusual reason for closing to traffic twice a year: thousands of snakes and other reptiles need to
articles.body: A road in southern Illinois, United States, has an unusual reason for closing to traffic twice a year: thousands of snakes and other reptiles need to cross it during their seasonal migration. Known as Snake Road, the 4-kilometre stretch in Shawnee National Forest connects LaRue Swamp with the limestone cliffs of LaRue-Pine Hills. The animals travel towards the wetlands in spring to feed, mate and rest before returning to the cliffs in autumn for shelter. To protect them from passing vehicles, the US Forest Service closes the road during both migration periods, allowing visitors to explore it on foot.Why do thousands of snakes migrate across Snake Road twice a yearSnake Road lies between two important ecosystems in the Shawnee National Forest. To its west is LaRue Swamp, which forms part of the Mississippi River basin. To the east are the LaRue-Pine Hills, an area known for its limestone cliffs, which rise 46 metres above the surrounding landscape.The seasonal movement takes place as temperatures change. In spring, reptiles emerge from hibernation as the weather becomes warmer and travel towards the swamp, where they can feed, mate and rest. When autumn arrives and temperatures begin to fall, they return towards the limestone cliffs, which provide places to shelter from colder conditions.US Forest Service enforces two seasonal road closuresThe US Forest Service closes Snake Road during two periods each year to protect migrating wildlife. According to the BBC, the road is closed from 15 March to 15 May in spring and from 1 September to 30 October in autumn.The closure dates were established following an earlier conservation measure introduced in 1972. Initially, the road was closed for three weeks during both the spring and autumn migration periods. However, biologist and herpetologist Scott Ballard, who worked with the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, found that the migration lasted longer than the original closure period. The Forest Service subsequently extended the restrictions to cover the longer migration.Seasonal road closures protect snakes from deadly trafficThe seasonal closure is intended to prevent reptiles from being accidentally killed by traffic while crossing the road. Snakes and other cold-blooded animals can move particularly slowly during cooler periods, making it difficult for them to cross before vehicles approach.According to the BBC, the black asphalt can retain warmth during early mornings and evenings, but the reptiles may still move slowly. They also tend to stop when approached, including when a vehicle is coming towards them.The scale of the threat has also been documented in research. According to National Geographic, biologist Rich Siegel reported that almost one in four snakes he collected for a study had been killed by traffic. The seasonal road closure helps reduce this risk by removing vehicle traffic during the migration periods.More than 23 snake species inhabit the Snake Road areaMore than 23 species of snakes have been recorded in the area, according to biologist Mark Vukovich, as reported by 5Chicago. The location is also home to several other reptiles and amphibians that use the route during their seasonal movements.Three of the snake species found in the area are venomous: the northern cottonmouth (Agkistrodon piscivorus), the copperhead (Agkistrodon contortrix) and the timber rattlesnake (Crotalus horridus). Other species that visitors may encounter include southern leopard frogs, different types of toads and salamanders, as well as turtles and lizards.These animals use the road as a passage between the two habitats. Their seasonal movement is the reason the Forest Service maintains restrictions on vehicles during specific months of the year.Visitors can explore Snake Road on foot during seasonal closuresAlthough vehicles are prohibited during the seasonal closures, visitors are permitted to walk along the 4-kilometre stretch of Snake Road to observe the migrating wildlife. However, sightings are not necessarily as frequent as some visitors might expect.Scott Ballard explained that visitors should not expect to see large numbers of snakes crossing the road simultaneously. He said, "If you see twenty snakes while you're out here, that's a good day."Visitors are advised to observe the reptiles from a safe distance and avoid approaching, handling or startling them. Collecting reptiles is also prohibited under federal and state law.The seasonal closure allows snakes, amphibians and other reptiles to move between LaRue Swamp and the LaRue-Pine Hills without vehicle traffic during their migration. By restricting access to cars during these periods, the Forest Service protects wildlife travelling along one of the United States' most unusual roads.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: China’s Xi says Taiwan ‘reunification’ must happen as history cannot be stopped
articles.summary: The tide of history cannot be stopped, Chinese President Xi Jinping said Thursday, as he urged complete “reunification” of Taiwan with the motherland and pledged to do so peacefully, making no mention of the use of force.
articles.body: BEIJING — The tide of history cannot be stopped, Chinese President Xi Jinping said Thursday, as he urged complete “reunification” of Taiwan with the motherland and pledged to do so peacefully, making no mention of the use of force. China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, despite Taipei’s strong rejection of that claim, and has repeatedly offered a “one country, two systems” model of autonomy not supported by any major Taiwanese political party. Resolving the Taiwan question is an “unwavering historical mission” of China’s Communist Party, Xi said in a speech in Beijing’s Great Hall of the People. “The tide of history cannot be stopped,” Xi added. “The complete reunification of the motherland must be realized, and it will certainly be realized.” Taiwan’s government dismissed the remarks as nothing new. “As for the wording on Taiwan unification, it isn’t much different from the past,” said Liang Wen-chieh, spokesperson for Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council. Xi’s comments came in a speech on the 160th birthday of revolutionary hero Sun Yat-sen, who helped lead a 1911 revolt that ended centuries of rule by emperors and empresses and ushered in the Republic of China. Xi said China adheres to “peaceful reunification and the policy of ‘one country, two systems’” and is willing to talk to Taiwan while upholding the “one-China principle,” or Beijing’s position that both sides of the Taiwan Strait are one country. All Chinese, including those in Taiwan, should join hands to jointly oppose Taiwan independence “separatist” forces and strive for peaceful development of cross-Strait ties, Xi added. Despite Xi not mentioning the use of force, which China has never renounced for Taiwan, its military operates around the island on a daily basis, and is extending its reach further into the Pacific. Taiwan’s defense ministry said it had detected 29 Chinese military aircraft, including J-16 fighter jets and drones, carrying out a “joint combat readiness patrol” around Taiwan in conjunction with Chinese warships starting Thursday. Xi’s speech comes a week ahead of the APEC summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, where he is due to again meet U.S. President Donald Trump, and also a little more than two weeks before important local elections in Taiwan. Last month, Taiwan called on its people to steer clear of any of China’s events to mark the Sun anniversary, saying China had a distorted view of him and his legacy. Beijing calls Sun a great national hero and patriot, as well as the forerunner of the 1949 communist revolution that forced the defeated Republic of China government to flee to Taiwan, where it remains to this day. Xi said Sun was a great national hero, a great patriot and a “great pioneer of China’s democratic revolution.” “Mr. Sun Yat-sen consistently upheld the unity of the country and the solidarity of the nation, and he firmly opposed all words and actions that split the country or the nation,” he added. In Taiwan, Sun is officially considered the “father of the nation” and his portrait hangs in the presidential office, though his political philosophy, “Three Principles of the People,” is no longer a required text for schoolchildren. While Taiwan President Lai Ching-te and his governing Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, they have been striking a tougher tone with Beijing on the role of the Republic of China. Taiwan has been particularly upset by Beijing’s effort to claim credit for the victory in World War II, saying it was the Republic of China government that fought alongside the U.S. and its allies, as the People’s Republic of China did not exist at the time. China says Lai is a “separatist” and has refused to speak with him. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future.
